t: Introduction: topic, aim and plan
n: In this lecture we will consider blood loss and its forensic medical significance. Blood loss is one of the primary causes of death from mechanical injury. Here, not only the volume of blood but also the rate of loss is important. The volume leading to death is 40–50 per cent of the blood in the body, or 2–2.5 litres. Minakov spots under the endocardium of the left ventricle are regarded as a sign characteristic of acute blood loss.

t: Causes of death from mechanical injuries
n: We classify the causes of death from mechanical injuries. In a primary cause, death occurs shortly after the injury; in a secondary cause, somewhat later. There are 7 primary causes: among them blood loss, traumatic shock, embolism and aspiration of blood. Secondary causes include infectious complications, for example sepsis and tetanus, and also traumatic toxicosis. Sometimes secondary blood loss is also observed.

t: Blood loss: volume and rate
n: In blood loss, volume and rate are assessed together. Not only the volume of blood lost but also the rate of blood loss is of importance. If large arterial vessels are injured, acute blood loss develops. Massive blood loss is more than 50%, that is 2.5 litres or more; it usually proceeds more slowly, over several hours. Attention, there is a risk of error: acute blood loss is rapid and relatively small in volume, whereas massive blood loss is slow and large in volume. They are not the same.

t: Volume of blood leading to death
n: About the volume of blood leading to death. Death occurs when 40–50 per cent of the blood in the body, or 4–4.5 per cent of body weight, is lost. If an adult loses 2–2.5 litres of blood, this causes death. According to Gubar's data of 1968, with a loss of 1–1.5 l of blood 33.3 per cent of victims may die, and with a loss of more than 2 l, 83.3 per cent. Pigolkin's textbook also notes that rapid loss of 2 l of blood or more usually leads to death. Attention: Giyasov defines massive blood loss as more than 50 per cent, that is more than 2.5 l; the threshold differs somewhat between sources.

t: Rate of blood loss: rate decides together with volume
n: About the rate of blood loss: rate decides together with volume. In the occurrence of death, the speed of bleeding is of great importance along with the amount of blood. With slow bleeding, a person may survive even after losing half of his blood. If bleeding from a vessel near the heart is rapid and relatively small, intracardiac pressure may fall or acute anaemia of the brain may develop, and death may occur. In injury to the aorta, carotid and femoral arteries, rapid death may occur even with a loss of less than 1 l of blood. The cause is not general exsanguination but a sharp fall in arterial pressure and bloodlessness of the brain. In slow, repeated bleeding, even if 2.5–3 l is lost, the possibility of resuscitation may be preserved.

t: Effect of age, sex and general condition
n: We look at the effect of age, sex and general condition. An adult has up to 5–6 l of blood; rapid loss of 2000–2500 ml of it usually leads to death. Young children are very sensitive to bleeding, because the volume of blood in their body is relatively small. A newborn may die even after losing 50–60 ml of blood. Women are less sensitive to blood loss than men. Children, the sick and the debilitated may die even from a small haemorrhage; death often results from blood loss, shock, cold and exhaustion.

t: Pathomorphology of acute blood loss
n: About the pathomorphology of acute blood loss. In injury of a large artery, even with bleeding of up to 500 ml, death occurs in the first minutes from ventricular fibrillation. In this case cadaveric lividity and rigor mortis are as usual. The diagram shows by organ: the brain and heart muscle are anaemic, while the spleen and other organs are as usual full of blood. Minakov spots under the endocardium of the left ventricle are a characteristic sign of acute blood loss.

t: Acute blood loss: signs and the mechanism of Minakov spots
n: We consider the signs of acute blood loss and the mechanism of Minakov spots. When the very largest vessels are injured, blood pressure falls so quickly that death occurs in the first minutes from ventricular fibrillation. In such rapid death, the picture of anaemia has no time to develop. On the corpse, signs of rapid death, traces of heavy bleeding, injury of a large vessel and Minakov spots are found. Minakov spots form because the blood pressure in the ventricular cavity is lower than in the capillaries.

t: Minakov spots
n: We will dwell separately on Minakov spots. These are band-like haemorrhages located under the endocardium of the left ventricle of the heart. They are regarded as a characteristic sign of acute blood loss. The cause of their formation is a sharp fall in intracardiac pressure and excessive irritation of the vagus nerve. Attention, there is a risk of error: in massive blood loss these spots are usually absent and are found only in some cases.

t: Pathomorphology of massive blood loss
n: About the pathomorphology of massive blood loss. Massive blood loss is loss of more than 50% of the blood, that is 2.5 litres or more. It usually proceeds more slowly, over several hours, and signs of general anaemia have time to develop. The skin is dry and pale. The internal organs, including the spleen, are found anaemic and contracted. Cadaveric lividity appears late and is less marked, whereas rigor mortis develops more strongly.

t: Later death: signs of anaemia and the microscopic picture
n: In later death: signs of anaemia and the microscopic picture. If death does not come very quickly and the blood depots have had time to empty, signs of acute anaemia appear. The skin and mucous membranes become pale; cadaveric lividity is pale, in the form of separate islands. The internal organs are pale and dry, the spleen is wrinkled; Minakov spots are found. Under the microscope, collapsed capillaries or capillaries filled with plasma, arteriolar spasm, leukostasis and leukocyte thrombi are seen. Later, because of hypoxia, cerebral oedema, hydropic dystrophy of neurons and nephrothelium, and then necrosis develop.

t: Corpse after death from massive blood loss (after Iskandarov)
n: A corpse after death from massive blood loss is described, after Iskandarov, as follows. The skin and mucous membranes of the corpse are markedly pale. Cadaveric lividity is weakly developed; the internal organs and muscles are anaemic and pale. Under the endocardium of the left ventricle, fine punctate or band-like haemorrhages characteristic of acute blood loss are seen, that is Minakov spots. In massive blood loss, cadaveric lividity is pale and appears as separate islands. In death from acute bleeding, signs of heavy bleeding may not be found; even then, the immediate cause of death is considered to be acute bleeding.

t: Comparing acute and massive blood loss
n: We compare acute and massive blood loss. In acute loss, a large arterial vessel is injured, the volume is up to 500 ml, and death occurs in the first minutes. In massive loss, more than 50% of blood is lost, the process lasts for hours and general anaemia develops. According to the table, in the acute form the spleen is as usual full of blood, cadaveric lividity is usual, and Minakov spots are characteristic. In the massive form the spleen is anaemic and contracted, cadaveric lividity is late and less marked, and Minakov spots occur only in some cases. Rigor mortis is usual in the acute form and stronger in massive blood loss.

t: Case analysis: arterial blood loss
n: Case analysis: arterial blood loss. A large artery is injured, and up to 500 ml of blood is lost. Death occurred in the first minutes from ventricular fibrillation of the heart. On the corpse only the brain and heart muscle are anaemic, while the spleen and other internal organs are as usual full of blood. Cadaveric lividity and rigor mortis are usual. Band-like haemorrhages, that is Minakov spots, are found under the endocardium of the left ventricle. Question: why do Minakov spots appear, and why does the spleen remain full of blood? Reason: intracardiac pressure falls sharply and the vagus nerve is excessively irritated.

t: Bleeding as a sign of vitality
n: Bleeding is regarded as a sign of vitality. Bleeding occurs only during life. Collection of blood at the scene, soaking of clothing, and accumulation of blood in cavities and tissues show that the injury was inflicted during life (vital). The finding of a Minakov spot also indicates that the injury occurred during life. Pooling of blood and soaking of clothing are taken into account as a sign of large blood loss, that is 1–2 l. Haemorrhage into tissues at the site of injury and somewhat further away is a sign of vitality, but by itself it is not sufficient for a correct conclusion.

t: Traumatic shock
n: About traumatic shock. Traumatic shock is the response to injury with severe disturbance of the nervous, cardiovascular and endocrine systems. In shock, peripheral circulation is insufficient, and the amount of circulating blood does not correspond to the capacity of the vascular system. The diagram shows the chain: injury, nervous and endocrine disturbance, disturbance of peripheral circulation, mismatch of blood volume with vascular capacity. Severe shock, that is grade III–IV, leads to death; in it venous congestion and depositing of blood in the liver and spleen are seen.

t: Internal bleeding: pelvic fracture and haemothorax
n: Internal bleeding: pelvic fracture and haemothorax. In pelvic injury, blood spreads between the soft tissues, into the retroperitoneal space, the gluteal and inguinal regions and the thigh. Here bleeding reaches 2.5–3 l and may be the immediate cause of death. Haemothorax is rarely seen in practice: with bleeding into the pleural cavity, death from massive blood loss occurs before severe respiratory failure develops. If, in a wound of a small-calibre artery, the bleeding is not stopped and help is not sought, death from massive blood loss may occur.

t: The role of blood loss in blast trauma
n: The role of blood loss in blast trauma. In blast trauma, massive blood loss, often associated with injury to limb vessels, is regarded as one of the immediate causes of death on day 1. Shock is also among the immediate causes of death on day 1. Secondary blood loss from erosive-ulcerative injury of the gastrointestinal tract is seen after day 60.

t: Compression by blood: haematoma, haemopericardium, haemothorax
n: Compression by blood: haematoma, haemopericardium and haemothorax. The brain and spinal cord, heart and lung may be compressed by blood or air; this is a complication of mechanical injury leading to death. In craniocerebral injury, haematomas are located within the bone, that is epidural, subdural and subarachnoid, and also intraventricular and in the brain tissue. When the cervical and thoracic parts of the spine are injured, these parts of the spinal cord are compressed. In chest injury, haemopericardium, pneumothorax and haemothorax develop. Attention: pneumothorax is related to air, haemothorax to blood.

t: Aspiration of blood and secondary causes
n: About aspiration of blood and secondary causes. In injury of the larynx and airways, and in fracture of the skull base and nasal bones, blood may enter the airways and lead to aspiration asphyxia. Secondary causes: purulent peritonitis, pleurisy, meningitis, osteomyelitis, gas gangrene, tetanus and traumatic toxicosis, which led to sepsis. Some time after the injury, secondary blood loss, shock and embolism may also be observed. Attention: in a primary cause death is rapid, in a secondary one it occurs after some time; do not confuse them.

t: Quick question: blood loss
n: We consolidate the topic with quick questions. First question: how does death occur in injury of a large artery, even with bleeding of up to 500 ml? Answer: in the first minutes, from ventricular fibrillation of the heart. Second question: where are Minakov spots found? Answer: under the endocardium of the left ventricle, as band-like haemorrhages; they are characteristic of acute blood loss. Third question: what is the volume of blood leading to death in an adult? Answer: 2–2.5 l, that is 40–50 per cent of the blood.

t: Case analysis: bleeding from a sharp object
n: Case analysis: bleeding from a sharp object. On the chest there is one stab wound of small external size, with scanty external bleeding. Question: if the wound is small and external bleeding is scanty, can the injury be called safe? Explain the reason. The guide is as follows: the external size of a stab wound is smaller than its depth, it penetrates the body cavity and increases internal bleeding. In addition: even with one external wound, the movement of the heart and lung may produce several internal injuries.

t: Conclusion and key concepts
n: Conclusion and key concepts. In injury of a large artery, even if up to 500 ml of blood is lost, death occurs in the first minutes from ventricular fibrillation. In acute loss, only the brain and heart muscle are anaemic, the spleen is as usual full; Minakov spots under the endocardium of the left ventricle are characteristic. In massive blood loss general anaemia develops: the skin is pale, the spleen is contracted, and cadaveric lividity is late and scanty. The lethal volume is 40–50 per cent of the blood, 2–2.5 l in an adult, but the rate and the calibre of the vessel may be decisive.
